extraction.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
extraction.description: A curated subset of 23 particularly challenging BIG-Bench tasks (27 subtasks) for which prior reported model results did not outperform the average human-rater score, released with prompts and Codex outputs for evaluating answer-only and chain-of-thought prompting.
extraction.creator: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei
extraction.rai:dataCollection: BBH was created by filtering BIG-Bench tasks using explicit criteria: limiting subtasks, requiring at least 103 examples, requiring human-rater baselines, restricting to multiple-choice or exact-match evaluation, keeping tasks where prior models did not beat average human-rater performance, excluding extremely difficult tasks, and then sampling evaluation examples.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some BIG-Bench tasks lacked human baselines, and some had only the minimum number of examples needed for submission; these were filtered out during curation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data came from BIG-Bench tasks, specifically over 200 diverse text-based tasks from the BIG-Bench benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was manipulated by filtering BIG-Bench tasks according to predefined criteria, excluding tasks outside scope, and randomly subsetting most tasks to 250 evaluation examples.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing consisted of filtering out tasks with more than three subtasks, fewer than 103 examples, without human-rater baselines, and without multiple-choice or exact-match metrics; then removing tasks where prior models beat average human raters and tasks deemed outside scope.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The authors manually wrote three chain-of-thought exemplars for each BBH task and prepended 'let's think step-by-step' to all CoT annotations in the few-shot exemplars.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human-rater baselines should be interpreted with care because they were not fully representative of human performance; task formatting and content changed over time, raters solved subsampled sets over many months, could use external resources, and some task descriptions were hard to follow.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that surpassing average human-rater performance on BBH should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning, and they avoided including Moral Permissibility because they did not want to delegate agency to models about moral judgment scenarios.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Some tasks require common practices and presuppositions in Western society, and human-rater scores are not representative of the entire population.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Human-rater baselines are not fully representative; task formatting and content changed during evaluation; some task descriptions were hard to follow; BBH excludes tasks requiring specialized knowledge or impractical effort; and even the best model still lags expert human-rater performance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation benchmark for measuring language model capabilities and limitations on challenging reasoning tasks, including few-shot answer-only prompting and chain-of-thought prompting comparisons.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Human-Rater Baseline Performance. Finally, we note that even though Srivastava et al. (2022) report the average and maximum of human-rater performances on most BIG-Bench tasks; the organizers acknowledge that one should be careful in interpreting these results because the scores are not fully representative of human performance. The human-evaluation component of the benchmark took almost a year, during which the formatting and content of some tasks had been changed multiple times. Human-raters were allocated a few hours per day to solve a sub-sampled evaluation set of a benchmark task, where they could use external resources such as the Internet.
